stories.headline: Google ships Gemini 4 Neon: #3 on the Artificial Analysis index at $3/$15, and it lands in Cursor the same day
stories.why_read: The top story on Hacker News with nearly 700 comments, and you retweeted Cursor's CursorBench numbers: this is the new cost-performance bar for coding agents.
body: Google DeepMind's Koray Kavukcuoglu introduced Gemini 4 Neon as frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across software engineering, knowledge work and science. Google says Neon scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, #3 overall and just behind larger, slower models, ranks #2 on the Vals Index and #2 on steerability on the new Agent Arena Index, and posted its lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Antigravity testing.

Pricing is $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 cached, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output, with a 1 million-token context window. It is rolling out in the Gemini API, Gemini for business, Antigravity for paid Pro and Ultra subscribers, and the Gemini app. Cursor added it immediately and says at default effort it scores 63.7% on CursorBench 4.1, up from 57.3% for Gemini 4 Hydrogen, setting a new cost-performance frontier there.

stories.headline: Musk at DealBook: Tesla will build an autonomous Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals for groups of six or seven
stories.why_read: You retweeted and bookmarked it: a second purpose-built robotaxi beyond Cybercab, aimed at families and groups.
body: Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit, Elon Musk said it will make sense for Tesla to build autonomous cars that seat different numbers of people. "We still need autonomous vehicles if you've got 4 or 6, or a whole family," he said, describing an autonomous version of the Model Y "that won't have steering wheels or pedals and would be good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people."
That fills the obvious gap in a fleet built around the two-seat Cybercab: airport runs, family trips and group rides. No timeline or production details were given in the clip Sawyer Merritt shared.

stories.headline: Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 a share and starts trading on Nasdaq today as ANT
stories.why_read: The largest stock debut ever by X's tally and a 498-comment HN thread; you bookmarked Uday Kotak's take that it now outweighs India's top 10 companies combined.
body: Anthropic, PBC priced 980 million Class A shares at $83.00, of which 956,351,354 are sold by the company and 23,648,646 by selling stockholders. Trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under "ANT" is expected to begin November 19, with closing expected November 20, and underwriters have a 30-day option on up to 147 million more shares. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are listed for the prospectus.

X's news summaries put the raise above $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion fully diluted valuation, with a $26 billion private placement that includes $10 billion each from Nvidia and Google at the IPO price. Uday Kotak noted that a company that did not exist about five years ago is now listed at $1.5 trillion, more than the top 10 Indian companies combined.

stories.headline: Two critical unauthenticated RCEs in NGINX's HTTP/2 code, one reaching back to 1.9.5 in 2015
stories.why_read: The most upvoted story on HN today at 1,400+ points: if you run NGINX with HTTP/2 on, patch first and read the rest after.
body: Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7 and Xint independently found two remote code execution flaws in NGINX itself, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 and both rated Critical at CVSS 4.0 9.2. Both require HTTP/2 to be enabled, and apps can be exposed even when their own code is secure. Wiz says NGINX powers more than 225 million websites.

Wiz reported the HTTP/2 use-after-free on October 21 with a working RCE and ASLR bypass, and F5 said another team had already reported it. The second bug was reported November 16, and both fixes went into F5's November 18 security release. The guidance is simple: find your NGINX deployments and update to the latest release.

stories.headline: Ruby2Shell: a one-byte heap overflow from upcasing 'ß' gives pre-auth RCE on stock Rails
stories.why_read: A second front-door bug on the same day: it hits default Rails and Sinatra, and bundled Ruby in GitLab and GitHub Enterprise Server.
body: Veria Labs traced the bug to Ruby's single-byte encodings, which have no capital ß. Upcasing writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one; the output buffer is input length plus 20 bytes, so 21 ß characters overflow it by one byte. The loop sits in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and dates to Ruby 2.4.0, reachable through upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different path.

Rails and classic-style Sinatra are affected in default configuration. Fixed Rubies are 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10. Veria's table lists GitLab 19.6.0 and GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 as still shipping affected Rubies, while Mastodon, OpenProject and Discourse are fixed. Ruby also posted a separate advisory on multiple Regexp and string case-conversion vulnerabilities.

stories.headline: Musk says Anthropic will likely keep renting SpaceX compute and wants an additional 10 gigawatts
stories.why_read: The compute story behind the IPO: the frontier labs' bottleneck is power, and SpaceX is selling it.
body: At the DealBook Summit, Musk said Anthropic is extremely likely to keep renting compute from SpaceX and wants significantly more, with its top plan calling for an additional 10 gigawatts. X's summary says that counters reports the deal might end after mid-2027, and points to Anthropic filings showing up to $120.5 billion in commitments through 2029.

The same summary says SpaceX is ramping AI infrastructure toward more than a gigawatt per month by late 2027. Read it together with the chip financing and StarMind stories below: SpaceX is positioning itself as a compute supplier, on the ground and in orbit.

stories.headline: Apollo arranges $40 billion off-balance-sheet financing so SpaceX can lease AI chips
stories.why_read: How the compute build-out actually gets paid for, and a peek at SpaceX's orbital-compute timeline.
body: According to X's news summary, Apollo Global Management is setting up a special-purpose vehicle that buys the chips and leases them to SpaceX for about five years, starting with $20 billion upfront, with deliveries set for early 2027. The structure lets SpaceX scale compute quickly while protecting its investment-grade rating.

CFO Bret Johnsen described ambitions for orbital compute satellites by 2027 and gigawatt-scale operations by 2029, with payback under a year. The summary also notes David Tepper's fund raising its SpaceX stake 1,626%.

stories.headline: Musk: the StarMind AI satellite is an easier problem than Starlink V3, mostly solar panels and a radiator
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: first-principles physics on why orbital inference may not be as hard as skeptics think.
body: Musk said he is not sure why people think an AI satellite would be hard, given SpaceX already has over 11,000 satellites in orbit. Starlink V3 is "an incredibly complex orbital radio station" with the most advanced phased-array antennas ever made, he said, while StarMind, the name for SpaceX's overall compute system, "really just consists of a very large array of solar panels and a radiator", with about five times as much solar area as radiator area.

At the center sits a compute module he described as about a quarter the physical size of a Vera Rubin NVL rack with the capability of a Vera Rubin NVL72. Shaun Maguire, also retweeted by you, put it more bluntly: last weekend's ship catch all but guarantees Starship works, and almost all inference compute will end up in space.

stories.headline: Microsoft AI launches seven models at Ignite, led by price-performance claims against GPT-6 and Opus 5.5
stories.why_read: Over 350 HN comments: a big incumbent competing on cost per task, the metric that matters when agents run all day.
body: Microsoft AI says token spend is skyrocketing and developers want models cheap enough to run agents 24/7 on real engineering work, so it released a family of seven. Its claims: MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra's quality at under 2% of the cost per task on CyberGym-E2E; MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's coding quality at about 40% of the price and 96% of Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price.

MAI Code 2 Flash is pitched as comparable to GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price and Haiku 5.5 at 20%, and MAI Image 2.7 is listed as #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing. These are vendor numbers; the HN thread is where the independent pushback lives.

stories.headline: Genie 4 rolls out to Google AI Ultra: real-time world editing by prompt, native audio and a community gallery
stories.why_read: Interactive world models are leaving the demo stage; a fun one to try if you have Ultra.
body: Google DeepMind and Google Labs are rolling Genie 4 out to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie. You can edit generated environments in real time with natural language, add native audio, and publish creations to a new gallery for others to explore and remix. Pro members can join a waitlist.
There is also a Project Genie agent that builds custom worlds through conversation, and an updated Genie 3 that supports longer sessions, panorama grounding and linked world sequences.

stories.headline: RadixArk's DaisyRose-27B doubles Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.1 with 1,200 tasks and 144 H200s
stories.why_read: An open-weights post-training recipe on a small budget, with BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 checkpoints you can run.
body: RadixArk's first model is built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens. It used just 1,200 curated tasks over 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs, and lifts Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%, with gains on other reasoning, instruction-following and coding benchmarks too.

The tasks were built with Eigent AI and selected so each targets a mistake the original model makes; about 1,200 of thousands of candidates made the cut. RadixArk credits three ingredients: high-quality training data, an efficient training backend and robust sandboxes.

stories.headline: Grok 4.8 is in RL with soft rollouts to some Grok Bot users; Musk says a week or two more polish
stories.why_read: The next Grok model is already quietly behind some Grok Bots, which may explain sudden behavior changes.
body: According to X's news summary, Musk said on November 17 that Grok 4.8 is in the reinforcement learning phase, with soft rollouts to some Grok Bot users, and that a general release needs another week or two of polish, emphasizing real-world usefulness over benchmarks.
The summary says the team rewrote its training stack from scratch in C and C++, and that multiple variants are in beta with no final choice yet.

stories.headline: A Grok Bot explains why one power user's usage is so low: scripts do the grunt work, one bot per job
stories.why_read: You retweeted it, and it reads like a checklist for your own fleet: connectors first, browser last, quiet routines.
body: Mike Pat asked his Grok Bot why his usage might be lower than others', and it listed the reasons. A Mac Mini runs scripts that scan texts, total a food log, pull robotaxi stats and sort promos, handing the bot only results. Long jobs like video renders and voice generation run there too, and some work goes to Hermes on his Claude plan so it never touches Grok Bot usage.

The rest is discipline: routines stay quiet unless something is wrong, each bot has one job with its own smaller context, preferences live in Notion and memory so nothing gets rebuilt, and connectors come first with the browser last because driving a browser costs far more.

stories.headline: KPMG's trial of 100+ AI agents on a FTSE 250 audit found they sometimes asked better questions than the human team
stories.why_read: A concrete enterprise result for agentic AI in a deeply manual profession, with a 224-comment HN debate.
body: KPMG UK ran more than 100 AI agents in an experiment codenamed Project Exponential, reported by the Financial Times, examining the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The agents worked alongside a conventional audit team across the audit process rather than on isolated admin tasks.

KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology in several instances went considerably deeper into issues than the regular team, flagging areas needing further investigation. The open question the piece raises is how fast that changes the economics of auditing.

stories.headline: New benchmark: eight agents beat one, but teams that don't talk beat teams that do
stories.why_read: A useful corrective for multi-agent designs: more chatter between bots can hurt.
body: Bespoke Labs launched the Multi Agent Coordination Bench, testing frontier models such as Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon on 12 complex tasks, including Mars missions, air traffic control and zombie defense, per X's news summary.

Eight agents averaged 0.42 against 0.35 for a single agent, but non-communicating teams scored 0.44, so communication often hurt; only Opus gained from messaging. CEO Mahesh Sathiamoorthy argues better coordination could unlock agent swarms for science and engineering.

stories.headline: Linger, from an early DeepSeek member, runs an open-source agent with persistent memory entirely on your own machine
stories.why_read: Private, subscription-free agents on an RTX 3060 or an Apple silicon Mac: the local-LLM crowd's answer to cloud bots.
body: Per X's news summary, Tony Zhang's Linger runs open models like Qwen and DeepSeek on consumer hardware, with persistent memory over local files, email and calendars plus multi-agent workflows for complex tasks. Benchmarks cited show 45.5 tokens per second on big models.
Enthusiasts are pairing it with tools like Jan and LocalAI, part of a broader push for AI the user fully controls.

stories.headline: Two decades of hacking, now with agents: a practitioner's LLM-assisted reverse-engineering workflow
stories.why_read: Practical agent craft that transfers to any long task: make the agent write its findings to markdown as it goes.
body: The author points an agent at a binary with a set of dedicated agent skills, using DeepSeek's harness with DeepSeek v4.1 Flash (occasionally Codex), Ghidra with an MCP bridge, and the radare2 and kuna CLIs, which are faster and possibly easier for AIs to drive. Current AIs, he notes, do fairly well with pure x86 or ARM disassembly.

The key habit is having the agent document every finding in MD files. Those notes help you understand the binary, keep the agent on track after compaction or a handoff to another agent, and stop it going in circles.

stories.headline: Netlify rebrands around prompt-to-app agents and projects 130% growth to $130M ARR
stories.why_read: A web-hosting incumbent reinventing itself around agents, with real usage numbers.
body: Per X's news summary, Netlify revealed a platform where users prompt AI agents in plain language to build apps with live previews, connected to over 150 tools like Notion and Stripe. CEO Matt Biilmann called it a full turnaround after years of flat growth.

The company projects 130% year-over-year growth and $130 million ARR by the end of 2026. In the past month, 500,000 people ran 1.7 million agent sessions, producing over 700,000 live deployments, and it saw 100,000 signups in a single day.

stories.headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion to push AI-designed drugs toward the clinic
stories.why_read: Big money on AI for chemistry and biology, still waiting on its first approved therapy.
body: According to X's news summary, Isomorphic Labs, founded by Demis Hassabis and spun out in 2021, closed an oversubscribed Series C co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia, with new backing from Andreessen Horowitz plus Alphabet. It follows a $2.1 billion raise earlier in 2026.

The money scales its IsoDDE engine, which predicts protein interactions, and more than 20 programs with partners like Eli Lilly and Novartis, pushing preclinical work in oncology and immunology toward trials. Separately, MIT spinout Boltz raised $110 million led by Bessemer for its open-origin biomolecular design models.

stories.headline: The new Tesla Roadster goes on public display at the LA Auto Show starting November 20
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: the first chance for the public to see the new Roadster in person.
body: Sawyer Merritt, citing the LA Auto Show, says the new Tesla Roadster will be on display at the show starting Friday, November 20.
If you have friends in LA, this is the weekend to get a closer look.

stories.headline: Tesla FSD sheds 71 to 26 mph when a deer bounds across a dark motorway
stories.why_read: You retweeted and bookmarked it: a split-second save that's hard to imagine a human making at night.
body: Nate shared a clip in which a deer leaps out of the dark across a motorway and Tesla FSD brakes from 71 to 26 mph, so the animal lives to leap another day. His question to viewers: would you have seen it?
The video originally came from kyfloyd; it is the kind of edge case robotaxi skeptics point to, handled here without drama.

stories.headline: Ship 42, the first Starship caught by the tower, won't fly again: Musk says it will be preserved for history
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: the caught ship becomes a museum piece.
body: Aaron Burnett relayed Musk's comment that SpaceX is not reflying Ship 42 and will preserve it for history.
Ship 42 made last weekend's tower catch after multiple orbits, a milestone X's summaries tie to Musk's renewed talk of rapid reuse and a Mars city.

stories.headline: Musk: TeraFab test chips by June, volume by late 2028, and an ArmyX crew recruited from In-N-Out and Starbucks
stories.why_read: A view into how the chip and data-center build-out gets staffed and scheduled.
body: Per X's news summary of his DealBook remarks, Musk expects first TeraFab test chips by June next year and volume production by late 2028 to feed AI infrastructure.

He also described ArmyX, a team recruited from fast food and retail for precise tasks such as running network cables, built by breaking complex jobs into simple, trainable steps so newcomers excel quickly alongside contractors.

stories.headline: Panasonic commits $1B+ to Sila's silicon anodes, the first US next-gen battery headed for commercial EVs
stories.why_read: You retweeted and bookmarked it: after years of false starts, a next-gen battery chemistry reaches real cars.
body: Steve LeVine reports in The Electric that Panasonic will buy more than $1 billion of silicon battery anodes from California startup Sila Nanotechnologies under a multi-year deal.
He calls it a big, long-awaited first: a US next-gen battery technology finally powering commercially sold electric vehicles.

stories.headline: Zerodha built Blobasaur, a sharded blob store on SQLite doing thousands of reads and writes a second
stories.why_read: A lovely boring-tech systems story: SQLite as the backbone of a distributed store for 20 million traders.
body: Kite, Zerodha's trading platform with about 20 million customers, stores user layouts, indicator templates, drawings and workspace preferences as opaque JSON blobs from a few KB to several MB. They moved from CouchDB to SSDB, a Redis-protocol C++ store, which ran reliably for years until it became unmaintained and was outside their stack.

Blobasaur, the replacement, is a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob server on SQLite that handles thousands of reads and writes per second on commodity hardware with single-digit millisecond latency.

stories.headline: Trying to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 1 core and 10GB, using smoltcp, DPDK and AF_XDP
stories.why_read: A playful, from-the-syscalls-up tour of high-performance networking.
body: The author's tongue-in-cheek goal is a web server for everyone on the planet, starting with 15 million on a single VM with 10GB of RAM and one CPU core. Instead of vibe coding it, the post rebuilds the idea from first principles, starting with the listen, accept, recv, send and close syscalls in plain C.
The title names the rest of the toolkit for getting there: userspace TCP with smoltcp and fast packet paths with DPDK and AF_XDP.

stories.headline: Take Voyager 1 apart, down to a single memory chip, in an interactive explorer
stories.why_read: A beautiful Show HN for the week Voyager 1 hit one light-day from Earth.
body: Raj Shekhar's site shows where the two Voyagers, launched in 1977 and still talking to Earth from interstellar space, are right now, and lets you replay the journey from launch.
The best part is the teardown mode: open the spacecraft bay by bay, then module by module, down to individual chips, with keyboard controls to move, turn and zoom.

stories.headline: Cambridge Dictionary names 'human' its Word of the Year 2026
stories.why_read: A gentle, very 2026 choice: what it means to be human when AI blurs the line.
body: The Cambridge Dictionary picked 'human' as Word of the Year 2026, framing the choice around a year of global debate about what it means to be human as AI blurs the boundaries between people and machines.
The pick lands in a year of agents, bots and AI coworkers, and the HN thread has more than 200 comments on whether it is insight or marketing.

stories.headline: Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa plans to rescind Abbott's H-1B executive order, and told Trump Big Bend wants monitoring, not a wall
stories.why_read: You retweeted it twice: a home-state policy shift that matters to Texas tech workers.
body: In a Texas Tribune interview in Austin, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa said she spoke with President Trump about border security on Saturday and told him Texans near Big Bend National Park would rather have electronic monitoring than a border wall. "He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border," she said.
Jasper Scherer highlighted that she plans to rescind several of Greg Abbott's executive orders, including those on H-1B visas and THC.

stories.headline: Austin foundry Digital Metal pours its leftover stainless steel into one-piece bottle openers
stories.why_read: You retweeted and bookmarked it: a small, clever bit of manufacturing thrift from your own city.
body: Connor Kapoor says Digital Metal makes the fastest castings in the west from its new foundry in Austin. When it casts stainless steel for a customer order it often melts more than needed, and instead of pouring the excess into ingot molds for revert, it now pours it into standby molds for one-piece bottle openers.
They are its first merch item, in 17-4PH or 304 stainless.
